extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, comic writers, literary critics, and students of drama
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing, evaluating, and understanding comedy (especially stage comedy and comedy of manners): the essay identifies qualities of the comic spirit, how comedy should be constructed, audience conditions, moral aims, style and character-drawing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of a cultivated audience
rubrics_metrics.description: The Comic poet requires 'a society of cultivated men and women ... wherein ideas are current and the perceptions quick' so that he may be supplied with matter and an audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy flourishes only where there is moderate intellectual activity; semi-barbarous or feverish emotional periods and marked social inequality of the sexes repel the comic poet. This explains why great comic poets are rare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtlety and delicacy of comic touch
rubrics_metrics.description: To touch and kindle the mind through laughter 'demands more than sprightliness, a most subtle delicacy' and is a natal gift in the Comic poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comic aim is at the head (intellect), not merely the sides or body; wit must penetrate the mind rather than deliver crude, physical jests. Lacking subtlety the poet's work will show a 'startling exhibition of the dyer's hand.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence between poet and audience acuity
rubrics_metrics.description: A corresponding acuteness must exist in the audience to welcome subtle comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even subtle comic writing fails if the audience lacks intellectual receptivity; the poet and audience must be matched in perception for the comic effect to land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pandering to extremes (agelasts or hypergelasts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy should not be aimed at non-laughers (agelasts) nor at excessive laughers (hypergelasts) who laugh at everything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neither extreme appreciates the Comic of Comedy: agelasts will not respond, while hypergelasts 'laugh at everything' and thereby lack appreciation of the distinctive comic of a well-crafted comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steer between Puritan and Bacchanalian reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage comedy must navigate opponents who view theatre either as immoral (Puritans) or as licence to vulgarity (Bacchanalians).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good comic practice involves positioning at a middle distance between inveterate opponents and over-enthusiastic supporters; a measured approach preserves dignity and audience reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe manners and stamp characters with their appropriate colour (Moliere's precept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy should 'observe the manners of his age and give his characters the colour befitting them at the time'—seize characters for the central purpose of the play and generalize them so as to be permanently human.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not paint in raw realism; slightly raise and soften particulars into generalized types that illuminate social truths and remain relevant beyond their immediate occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy must have an idea / central purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The life of a high comedy is 'in the idea'—a central conception that animates character and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot without idea is thin; mere farce and repeated situations (stock epigrams) are inferior. The comic action should serve and express a sustained intellectual or social insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer generalization over raw realism
rubrics_metrics.description: Realistic comedy that is mere 'incessant remuage' (bustle without thought) is inferior; the comic poet should generalize upon character-examples rather than present unvarnished realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Realism may age out of sympathy as society improves; true comedy abstracts and elevates particulars to reveal permanent aspects of human nature (contrast Moliere vs. purely realistic or vulgar portrayals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit source: clear reason and common-sense, not mere flash
rubrics_metrics.description: The best wit 'is of clear reason: it is a fountain of that soil; and it springs to vindicate reason, common-sense, rightness and justice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid surface 'prepared' bon-mots or gimmicky wordplay that exist only to dazzle; prefer wit that arises organically from character and idea (contrasts drawn between Moliere's running-brook wit and Congreve's bully-fencer wit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic integration of moral and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A comedy's moral must be 'in the heart of his work, throbbing with every pulsation of an organic structure' rather than a preachy tail or an obvious appended lesson.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not hang morality 'like a tail' or preach through a character constantly cocking an eye at the audience. The instructive element should emerge naturally from the play's construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cynical licentiousness and base corruption of comic licence
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier English imitations sometimes added cynical licentiousness to comic licence, producing a worse vice than frank filth; a noble entertainment spoiled by wretched taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic licence (the right to bold utterance) should not descend into cynical immorality; maintain self-mastery and purity of conception even when wielding a 'shrieking scourge' upon vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and vigour over stale stock situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy that repeats the same situations at second hand becomes tiresome; original study and vigour of conception are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid recycling Scene v. Act 2 of Misanthrope ad nauseam (Wycherley, Congreve, Sheridan). The comic poet must produce fresh material reflective of his time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy as social instruction (exposing causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy can teach the world to understand what ails it by exposing causes (example: Femmes Savantes ridiculed excessive purism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful comedy not only amuses but clarifies social follies, sometimes requiring repeated exposure before public taste changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-drawing: stamp types for permanence without caricature
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be drawn 'firmly for the central purpose of the play' and generalized to be 'permanently human,' not mere puppets or painted faces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for portraits that convey individuality and type simultaneously (Moliere, Menander, Shakespeare examples); avoid shallow or purely artificial types that fail to move the sympathetic mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the real world and human nature; don't expect too much
rubrics_metrics.description: To love and understand Comedy one 'must know the real world, and know men and women well enough not to expect too much of them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic insight requires observation and realistic understanding of human shortcomings; the comic poet's aim is to reveal and refine, not to moralize from an idealized distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper role and prominence for women in comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: High comedy 'is the fountain of sound sense' and gives women prominent, witty parts (e.g., Dorine, Celimene, Millamant) that showcase common-sense and intellectual parity with men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write female characters with wit and agency; Comedy elevates women by offering them significant comic roles rather than passive romantic idiocy.
